p.title: Systemic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying

ext.title: Systemic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
ext.document_type: Journal article manuscript (working version dated December 6, 2023). The journal is not named in the text. The metadata hint's DOI 10.1086/734531 does not appear in the text, so it is not confirmed here.

Read via a filtered copy at C:\Users\pgoff\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-pgoff-OneDrive-Desktop-Melange-Systems\693e1754-6a96-45a9-b931-f03762acbd89\scratchpad\kim_filtered.txt (3,562 lines). The only lines removed were blank lines and lone "G" figure-node residue lines from the PDF extraction. Everything else was read: main text pp.1-29, references, Appendices A-L, and all tables. Stray merge-marker text ("HEAD ====== 19eac...") appears in the PDF extraction at about p.24; it is an extraction artifact, not content. Paul's markup: no annotation file was found for this document (checked _annots and annotations), so paul_markup is empty. Network, path-finding, allocation, persuasion/turnout and text-measurement topics are not analyzed as such. The paper uses a firm-politician bipartite graph descriptively (Fig.1, App.F) and matches bills by number and title (p.11, fn.9).
ext.research_question: Do special-interest groups (mainly publicly traded firms, their corporate PACs and their employees) donate to members of Congress whom they later lobby on related bills? The paper tests a sequential "access-buying" link: a first-time donation to a politician is followed by lobbying on bills sponsored by, co-sponsored by, or assigned to committees of that same politician.
ext.theory: Access-buying hypothesis: donations secure access to legislators, and lobbying then informs them or shapes content (pp.5-6). Alternatives discussed: electoral and ideological motives (Poole and Romer 1985); legislative subsidy (Hall and Deardorff 2006); donations as rewards after favorable action (Snyder 1990, tested in App.K). Three hypotheses (pp.6-8): (H1) donors lobby bills the politician sponsors; (H2) donors lobby bills the politician co-sponsors; (H3) donors lobby bills assigned to the politician's committees, the strongest link expected. Corporate PAC donations are expected to show a stronger link than employee or CEO donations.
ext.data: Main sample: publicly traded US manufacturing firms (NAICS 2-digit 31-33) and all members of Congress serving 2008-2018 (979 members, 2,703 firms). Unbalanced panel of 2,646,237 firm-politician dyads and 16,428,834 observations per text (p.15). Table 1 and App. H report N = 16,434,912, which does not match the text; flagged in limitations. Unit: firm-politician-year dyad. Lobbying source: LDA reports, over 1.2 million parsed, of which 1.27 million (1999-2020) are cited, with 0.25 million (about 20%) mentioning specific bills and covering about 97% of lobbying spending (pp.9-10). Donation source: FEC filings, over 75 million records since 1999 (abstract and p.11); about 53 million itemized individual contributions 1980-2018 (p.11). Interest-group coverage: over 84,000 groups (abstract; p.2). Other samples: 2013 cross-section of all public firms (9,791 firms, 597 members, 5,845,227 possible dyads; App.D); services firms (App.H.2, NAICS 42-81); 1999-2000 interest-group comparison (App.G); 111th Congress (2009-2010) Senate miscellaneous tariff bills (MTBs), 477 bills and 107 lobbying firms (App.L). Covariates from Volden and Wiseman (2018) and Compustat (sales, employees).
ext.method: (1) Linear probability model with fixed effects (Eq. 2, Table 1, App.H). Outcome: firm lobbies a bill tied to politician j in year t through sponsorship, co-sponsorship or committee. Treatment: first-time donation within a 3-year window (Eq. 1, L=3). Fixed-effect structures vary across columns: firm, year, politician, and firm-politician. Standard errors clustered by firm. (2) Difference-in-differences with matching (Eqs. 3-4, Figs. 4-5, Tables J.1-J.3). Each treated pair (i,j) with a first-time donation in t is matched to 10 nearest firms (Mahalanobis distance on sales, employees and lobbying up to t-1) that gave j no donation in t to t-3. Estimand: change from t-1 to t+F in the lobbying outcome, treated minus matched-control mean, averaged over treated pairs. 95% CIs from block bootstrap. Robustness: NAICS 3-digit matching (Table J.2), donor-type splits (Fig.5), lagged donations (Table H.5), lobbying-to-donation reverse test (App.K, Table K.1). (3) Descriptive comparisons with Ansolabehere, Snyder and Tripathi (2002) (App.D, E, G).
ext.identification: Within-politician comparison. Variation is across firm-politician pairs with the same politician, so politician-specific productivity and ideology are absorbed (p.2). The first-time-donation-in-3-years design separates new donations from ongoing ones and makes donation timing identifiable. The DiD assumes parallel trends: the matched controls' pre-period lagged outcome changes are constant (p.24). Covariate balance improves after Mahalanobis matching (App.I). Firm-politician alignment is handled by firm-politician FE (cols 4 and 8 of Table 1). Unobserved firm-politician-time shocks are not handled, and the authors say the estimates are not causal (pp.28-29).
ext.scope: Population: publicly traded US manufacturing firms (services and all-public-firm checks in appendices), lobbying and PAC/employee donations to members of Congress. Institution: US federal Congress (House and Senate), with lobbying under LDA and donations under FECA. Era: main analysis 2008-2018 (LDA electronic filing mandatory after the 2007 HLOGA amendment, p.15); descriptive work 1999-2020; the 1999-2000 comparison uses interest-group data. Results are observational and do not establish causation.

key_findings.finding: Firm-politician Table 1 OLS: a first-time donation within 3 years raises the probability that the firm lobbies a bill tied to the politician (sponsor, co-sponsor or committee) by 2.3 to 4.8 percentage points. Base rate of such lobbying is about 0.07.
key_findings.location: Table 1 and text, pp.19-20; FE-heavy col.4 coefficient 0.023

key_findings.finding: Matched DiD: donations raise the probability of lobbying a politician-linked bill, rising over time. Senate effect is about 8 pp at t+0, rising to about 11 pp at t+3; the House effect is larger.
key_findings.location: Figure 4, pp.25-26; Table J.1, p.17; text p.26
key_findings.numbers: Senate: 0.075, 0.097, 0.108, 0.110 (t+0 to t+3); House: 0.086, 0.111, 0.127, 0.127; Senate SE about 0.003-0.004, House SE about 0.002-0.003; 3,778 Senate and 5,497 House first-time donation instances

key_findings.finding: Corporate PAC donations show the strongest link to later lobbying, especially committee-related lobbying. Employee and CEO donations also show links, but smaller ones.
key_findings.numbers: Committee lobbying, PAC: 0.103 (t+0) rising to 0.147 (t+3); CEO 0.017 to 0.050; Employee 0.015 to 0.039. Sponsorship, PAC: 0.029 to 0.037; CEO 0.012 to 0.029; Employee 0.014 to 0.022. Co-sponsorship, PAC: 0.097 to 0.102. Table J.3 CEO co-sponsorship at t+2 is 0.28, which is far above the rest of its row and is not discussed in the text. Instance counts: PAC 2,662; CEO 792; Employee 934

key_findings.finding: Donations are followed by lobbying, not the reverse. Lobbying does not raise later donations, except a small effect of lobbying a bill's sponsor at t+0.
key_findings.location: Appendix K, Figure K.1, Table K.1, p.20-21 (text p.26)
key_findings.numbers: Lobby Sponsor t+0 coef 0.0074 (SE 0.0028); other lags and types near zero; 12,232,896 firm-politician-quarter dyads; lobby-sponsor instances 4,426

key_findings.finding: Donations and lobbying are concentrated. About 5% of public firms both donate and lobby, and they account for most political spending.
key_findings.location: Data section p.5; Table D.1, p.4 and p.6; App.D
key_findings.numbers: 2013: 518 of 9,791 public firms (5%) both donate and lobby, responsible for $2.6bn of $2.86bn (89%). Firm-politician dyads with both: 12,862 (less than 0.1% of 5,845,227) containing $520m (18%). About 4% of all dyads have any political link

key_findings.finding: Among firms that both lobby and donate, PAC donations and lobbying spending are positively and significantly associated (log-log).
key_findings.numbers: beta = 0.88, R2 = 0.39; text: a 10% PAC increase is associated with 8.8% more lobbying among firms that also lobby

key_findings.finding: Most donation-only links come from employees, not corporate PACs.
key_findings.numbers: 19,735 of 23,270 donation-only dyads in 2013 (about 85%) are created by employee donations

key_findings.finding: Miscellaneous tariff bills (MTBs), a descriptive success check: firms that lobby and donate to the senator from their state or to Senate Finance members see MTB approval more often than lobby-only firms. The paper calls the gap significant, but no test is reported.
key_findings.location: Appendix L, Table L.1 (duplicated as L.2), pp.24-26
key_findings.numbers: Lobby-only: 23 of 66 (0.348) approved. Lobby+donate: 17 of 41 (0.415). Difference 0.067 (+19%). 477 Senate MTBs in 111th Congress; 211 proposed by 46 public firms; 107 public firms lobbied on MTBs

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity by the dyad and group of interest: the paper says the donation-lobbying link is strongest for corporations, weaker for labor unions; this replicates Ansolabehere et al. (2002) using 1999-2000 data.
key_findings.numbers: Beta (cube-root PAC vs lobbying): corporations 2.0; membership organizations 1.6; trade associations 0.8; labor unions 0.6; no relationship for unions per text

limitations: Not causal. The authors say their estimates should not be read as causal and that the study shows an association (pp.3, 28-29). Donation timing may be driven by unobserved firm-politician-time shocks.
Lobbying is measured only through bill-linked reports: about 20% of 1.27 million reports cite bills. The authors call the results a lower bound (p.10).
Bill positions are reported for only about 17% of lobbied bills; 82% of those are supportive (fn.12, p.17).
Parallel trends are assumed; the authors check only that the lagged-outcome difference is roughly constant (p.24). Matching uses sales, employees and lobbying up to t-1 only.

Sample inconsistencies: text says 16,428,834 observations, while Table 1 and App. H report 16,434,912. The donation-amount effect is stated as 0.03 pp per 10%, which matches only the firm-politician-FE column (0.003), not col.5 (0.006).

Lobbying data quality: LDA reports lack unique bill IDs, reporting changed from semi-annual to quarterly in 2008, and the sample starts in 2008 for these reasons (fns.5, 9; p.15). Bill matching relies on cross-referencing bill numbers and titles.

Relationships may reflect the revolving door or association lobbying; lobbyists with covered positions are about 7.8% of lobbyists and their lobbying on sponsored bills is under 1% (fn.15). The authors argue this does not drive results.
Manufacturing focus: service firms give almost identical results (App.H.2). Donor types are correlated (p.27), so type-specific effects are not independent.

MTB analysis is one Congress (111th), descriptive, and small (41 vs 66 firms). No significance test is reported despite the word 'significant' on p.25. Table L.2 duplicates Table L.1 in the extraction.

Unit of donation treatment is first-time donation within 3 years; the authors note that first-time-ever donations give almost identical results (App.H.3-H.5), but this is not a test of a different identification.
measures: Outcome: binary firm-politician-year indicator that the firm lobbies a bill sponsored by, co-sponsored by, or assigned to a committee of politician j (Y^a_ijt, with a in {Sponsor, Co-sponsor, Committee}).
Treatment: first-time donation within 3 years (X*_ijt(L), L=3), and logged first-time donation amount.
Donor types: corporate PAC (PAC $), CEO/executive, and rank-and-file employee donations; government-relations staff donations used in App.E.
Lobbying spending: Lobby $ allocated across bills and politicians (App.C, a noisy measure; binary link used in main analysis).
Politician controls: party, majority status, committee chair, membership of top-4 powerful committees (Groseclose-Stewart scores), from Volden and Wiseman (2018).
Firm controls: sales and employees (Compustat); matching covariates: sales, employees, lobbying up to t-1 (Mahalanobis distance, 10 nearest).
Occupation codes: SOC 11-1011 (executives) and 27-3030 (public relations/government affairs) to classify employees; name matching via graph clustering and fastLink (Enamorado, Fifield and Imai 2019).
references_of_note: Ansolabehere, Snyder and Tripathi (2002), Business and Politics 4(2): the seminal PAC-lobbying link study that this paper replicates and extends (pp.1, 4-5, App.D, G).
Ansolabehere, de Figueiredo and Snyder (2003), JEP: donations are too small to buy politicians (pp.28-29).
Hall and Deardorff (2006), APSR: lobbying as legislative subsidy, the main alternative mechanism (p.6).
Kalla and Broockman (2016), AJPS: field experiment on donor access, the closest causal benchmark (p.4).
Powell and Grimmer (2016), JOP: money in exile, PACs seek short-term committee access (p.4).
Fowler, Garro and Spenkuch (2020), JOP: no quid-pro-quo returns to corporate PAC donations (p.29).
Huneeus and Kim (2019) and Kang (2015): corporate lobbying returns (pp.29, 28).
Snyder (1990), JPE: campaign contributions as investments, the reward-based alternative (p.6).
Esterling (2007) and Fouirnaies and Hall (2018): committee-directed access and buying expertise (pp.8, 4).
Stuckatz (2021) and Richter and Werner (2017): employee donations follow company PAC donations and CEO substitution (pp.8, 27).
Ludema, Mayda and Mishra (2018): MTB approvals used as the lobbying success outcome (p.22).
LaPira and Thomas (2020): LDA data limitations (fn.5).
Volden and Wiseman (2018): source of politician-level covariates (p.18).
Enamorado, Fifield and Imai (2019), APSR: fastLink record linkage used to match FEC and Govtrack IDs (p.12).

short_quotes.quote: previous donations are associated with an 8-11 percentage point increase in the likelihood of the targeted politician's involvement in lobbied legislative bills
we are not asserting a causal relationship between campaign donations and lobbying actions
our estimates should not be interpreted as causal

rel.summary_md:
Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters build a firm-politician-year panel. It covers 2,703 publicly traded manufacturing firms and 979 members of Congress from 2008 to 2018. Lobbying comes from parsed LDA reports that name bills, and donations come from FEC records. The question is whether a firm's first donation to a member in a 3-year window is followed by the firm lobbying bills that the member sponsors, co-sponsors, or that go to the member's committees.

**Fixed-effects results.** The models compare firm-politician pairs within the same politician. A new donation goes with a 2.3 to 4.8 percentage-point higher chance of that lobbying. The base rate is about 0.07. These are pooled estimates (UNSTRATIFIED by chamber or donor type).

**Matched difference-in-differences.** These results are split by chamber. Senate estimates rise from 7.5 pp at t+0 to 11 pp at t+3. House estimates rise from 8.6 to 12.7 pp.

**Donor type and channel.** The link is strongest for corporate PAC money and for lobbying tied to committees. For PACs, committee-linked lobbying rises from 0.103 to 0.147. CEO and employee donations show much weaker links, and lobbying does not predict later donations. Only about 5% of public firms both donate and lobby (2013).

**Limits.** The authors say plainly that the results are associations, not causal effects. The lobbying measure reaches the member only through who sponsors the bill or which committee gets it, because LDA filings never name members.

**What it means for Melange.**
- It is the closest published counterpart to the closed FEC x LDA bridge test. The paper uses a different unit (firm-member pairs over time, not a member-level cross-section) and different fixed effects.
- It also points to a gap. The paper's strongest channel, committee referral, is missing from the system's LobbyView outcome, which counts only sponsor and cosponsor links. And the system's own committee control may absorb that channel.
- It supports the engine's choice to measure money from direct PACs only, and the "money buys access" stance as a weak prior. It does not speak to votes or flips.

All of this is UNVERIFIED agent analysis until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Within-politician, first-time-donation designs find donations followed by lobbying on the member's bills: Table 1 coefs 0.023-0.048 (pooled, UNSTRATIFIED, N=16.4M firm-politician-years, 2008-2018); matched DiD Senate 0.075->0.110, House 0.086->0.127 (t+0..t+3; 3,778 Senate / 5,497 House instances). The committee channel is strongest (PAC committee 0.103->0.147 vs sponsorship 0.029->0.037). Lobbying does not predict later donations (App. K).
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 pp.19-20; Fig.4 and Table J.1 pp.25-26; Fig.5 and Table J.3 p.27; App. K
bearings.system_side: Bridge round 3 is a member-level cross-sectional correlation (Spearman). X is a member's FEC exposure for each industry and cycle. Y is LobbyView n_bills: lobbied bills the member sponsored or cosponsored, for 22 lob_ids in CU, fintech and crypto, 2023-26. Four controls: party, chamber, volume and committee. Raw rho +0.153; four-control partial -0.0002. Verdict UNCORROBORATED, route CLOSED for this window. The prereg itself already names an overcontrol reading: 'association present but not separable from committee structure'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's unit is the firm-member pair over time, with politician, firm and pair fixed effects and first-time donation timing. That design tests a different estimand from a member-level cross-section with a committee control. Because the paper finds the association runs mainly through committee-linked bills, the bridge's committee control plausibly absorbs the very channel the paper measures. So the round-3 null and the paper's positive estimates are not in conflict. Sample mismatch: the paper covers about 2,700 manufacturing firms in 2008-2018; the bridge covers 22 financial-sector clients in 2023-26. The paper is not causal either. Per the prereg, this cannot license re-running the bridge on the same window with different controls. It informs only a successor prereg on a new LobbyView vintage.

bearings.paper_claim: The outcome is a firm lobbying any bill tied to politician j through sponsorship, co-sponsorship or committee referral. Bills are matched by number and title, because LDA reports carry no member names and no unique bill IDs. Only about 20% of 1.27M reports cite bills; the authors call the results a lower bound.
bearings.paper_location: Eq.2 and pp.9-11, fn.5, fn.9, p.15
bearings.system_side: The member link is built by joining each lobbied bill to its sponsor/cosponsor roster ('did this organization lobby a bill this member sponsored or cosponsored'). P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction, so the link is REFUTED as evidence of influence or contact.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's outcome is the same roster-join construction, plus a committee-referral arm. It escapes the system's circularity only because its treatment is donation timing, not bill joining. It is still a measure of a member's involvement in lobbied bills, not of contact with the member. That matches the system's ruling that the join is not a contact measure. It gives no license to use the join as an influence edge (D-021). It does show a coverage gap: the system's roster has no committee-referral link.

bearings.paper_claim: Corporate PAC donations show the strongest sequential association with later lobbying of the recipient: committee lobbying 0.103->0.147, versus CEO 0.017->0.050 and employee 0.015->0.039. The authors frame this as consistent with access-buying. They state 'our estimates should not be interpreted as causal' (p.29). The amount effect is small (0.003 per 10% in the firm-politician FE column).
bearings.paper_location: Fig.5 and Table J.3 p.27; Table 1 col.4; pp.28-29
bearings.system_side: WM 0.35 / WP 0.65 is calibrated on the premise that money buys access and effort more than votes. Engine money comes only from direct PAC contributions (Schedule B 24K/24Z); individual contributions are out of scope. The money term is a saturating function of the amount relative to receipts, with no timing or first-donation feature.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper backs the 'money is about access' premise and the PAC-only scope: PAC money is the channel with the strongest association. It says nothing about roll-call flips, the quantity pflip models. Its outcome is the firm's lobbying behaviour, not the member's position. Sample is manufacturing firms 2008-2018, not CU or bank PACs. The evidence is associative. Treat it as a weak prior for the WM<WP choice, not an estimate of WM.

bearings.paper_claim: Of the three links (sponsor, co-sponsor, committee), committee-linked lobbying after a donation is the largest and grows over time (PAC 0.103->0.147, t+0..t+3). H3 predicts this because bills pass through committees; chair status enters only as a control.
bearings.paper_location: Hypotheses pp.6-8; Fig.5 p.27; Table J.3
bearings.system_side: Influence% = committee_raw/max, built from seat weights by CU-relevance tier (Highly 3.0 / Moderately 1.8 / Slightly 0.9, subcommittee 1/6) and leadership multipliers (Chair 3.0 full / 7.5 sub; Ranking 2.0 / 4.5).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the claim that interest groups concentrate money and lobbying on committee members. That is evidence that committee position is a structural target layer, in line with Paul's position. It does not estimate the chair/ranking ladder, the 1/6 subcommittee weight, or committee effects on CU bill outcomes. It shows where firms act, not whose action moves bills. Sample is manufacturing firms at federal level, 2008-2018.

bearings.paper_claim: Individual FEC donors are linked to firms and to Govtrack/FEC candidate IDs through constrained graph clustering and fastLink probabilistic record linkage (Enamorado, Fifield and Imai 2019). Executives and government-relations staff are classified with SOC occupation codes 11-1011 and 27-3030.
bearings.system_side: Same-name donor candidates are resolved by an ordered rule ladder: exact name + zip -> AUTO; cross-employer -> HIGH; nickname/same city, state + occupation and employer contradiction -> REVIEW; otherwise DISCARD. There is no name-frequency weighting.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Directly relevant: both systems face the same FEC problem of donors with no unique identifier. fastLink's frequency-weighted match scores would address the ladder's known blind spot, which is that common names in the same zip get AUTO. The paper reports no precision or recall for its linkage, so it offers a method, not a benchmark. Mentat's strict-names and exclude-on-contradiction rulings (D-040) still govern; any change is Paul's call.

gaps_exposed: The system's LobbyView member outcome (lob_id x bioguide x year n_bills) links members only as sponsor or cosponsor of a lobbied bill. It has no committee-referral arm, which is the channel where the paper's association is largest. Brain note lobbyview-collector.md:127 confirms edges = sponsor + all cosponsors.

No org x member panel over time: the bridge is a member-level cross-section with a committee control. Nothing in the system can separate a relationship's onset (a first donation) from continued giving, so the paper's within-politician, first-time-donation design has no counterpart.

Engine money features (flip_model, money_response) are amounts per two-year cycle relative to receipts. They have no timing or relationship-onset signal, even though the paper finds the binary first-donation indicator carries the association and the amount effect is small.
No reverse-direction check (lobbying followed by donations) exists alongside the bridge. The paper treats that check as a key way to rule out reverse causation (App. K).
flags: D-021: the paper builds a firm-politician bipartite graph from LDA bill mentions joined to sponsor, co-sponsor and committee rosters (Fig.1, App.F). Adopting those links as Melange edges or weights would breach D-021 (LDA is an identity source only) and reproduce the circular roster join (lobby_interactions.py:4).

Wording (D-025 family): 'access-buying' is the authors' hypothesis; the results are associations ('not causal', pp.3, 29). No figure from this paper may be presented as an access, closeness or introduction probability, or as donations causing lobbying.

Pooled-coefficient rule: Table 1's 2.3-4.8 pp estimates pool House and Senate and all donor types; quote them as UNSTRATIFIED (window 2008-2018, denominator 16.4M firm-politician-years). The chamber-stratified DiD (Senate 0.075-0.110, House 0.086-0.127) is the stratified figure.

Paper-internal inconsistencies: the text says N=16,428,834 while Table 1 and App.H report 16,434,912. Table J.3 has a CEO co-sponsorship value of 0.28 at t+2, out of line with its row. App. L calls the MTB gap (0.415 vs 0.348; 41 vs 66 firms) 'significant' without reporting a test.
Bridge closure: the round-3 prereg bars a different control set on the 2023-26 window as a successor. This paper supports only a successor prereg on a new LobbyView vintage, never a re-run.

Paul's media-blend note says Kim's effects fade within 2 to 3 years. This 2023 version shows estimates rising from t+0 to t+3 and stopping at t+3; it does not measure any fade. The note should not be used as a decay timescale for press/social half-lives or staffer-tie decay.
Neither rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization) is argued in this paper.
All bearings are new agent analysis and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's core expectation that donations precede lobbying. It does so at the firm-member level, within the same politician, and as an association only. It is also consistent with Furnas's low overlap: only about 5% of public firms both donate and lobby. The system's closed bridge null does not contradict the paper. That test uses a member-level cross-section with a committee control, a different unit and possibly an overcontrol of the paper's strongest channel. Paul's notes do not record this distinction. His committee-pillar position (money and lobbying effects strongest in committee activity) is supported in direction. The paper says nothing about the pillar's weights. His annotation for media-blend and access-uncertainty, that Kim's effects fade within 2 to 3 years, is stale or inaccurate for this version: the estimates rise through t+3 and no fade is measured. The annotation names this work as JOP 2026; the PDF read here is a December 2023 working version, and the journal and DOI are not confirmed in the text.

related.why: An earlier working version of the same project, with the same authors, data and first-time-donation design. This 2023 version adds the matched DiD and the appendices.

Furnas finds low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending. This paper's 2013 figure, 518 of 9,791 public firms (5%) doing both, is consistent with that, and its sequential finding applies only within that overlap.
A randomized field experiment on whether contributions open access. This paper cites it (p.4) as the closest causal benchmark for its observational access-buying association.
LobbyView's firm-level bill-linked LDA parsing is the lobbying source here. It is also the source of the system's lob_id network and its bridge outcome.
Imai and Kim's cautions on two-way fixed effects and matched DiD apply directly to this paper's FE LPM and matched DiD, and to any successor design for the bridge.
This paper has bill positions for only about 17% of lobbied bills. Kim 2025's LLM-derived positions on the same LobbyView data would let a donation-lobbying link be signed by support or opposition.
The same LobbyView firm-politician bipartite construction from bill sponsorship, used for community detection instead of sequential timing.
Cited (pp.28-29) as evidence on firm-level returns to lobbying. It shares the In Song Kim lineage and LobbyView firm data.
A review of empirical lobbying models that places the access-buying and legislative-subsidy mechanisms this paper weighs.

paul_entries.text:
Kim, In Song, et al. “Systemic and sequential links between campaign donations and lobbying.” *The Journal of Politics*, vol. 88, no. 1, 1 Jan. 2026, pp. 110–124, [https://doi.org/10.1086/734531](https://doi.org/10.1086/734531).

“*Specifically, we find that previous donations are associated with an increase of* ***8–11 percentage points*** *in the likelihood of the targeted politician’s involvement in lobbied legislative bills. The estimated effects are large, increase over time, and are particularly pronounced for committee-related activities.*” This article is very pertinent to the present discussion as it directly tests the likelihood that a representative is to be influenced by an advocacy group under the pretext of past political contributions. Importantly, the author describes the observed phenomena as something that compounds but quickly fades, as the observed longevity of such favor granted by a political donation is pronounced for only **6 months**, but then fades soon after, unless renewed which then such favor is compounded upon.
